tip: After domandare, a reported question can turn subjunctive: perché non fossi venuto, not the plain 'non sei venuto'.
For English 'would come' in reported speech, Italian uses the past conditional: Ha detto che sarebbe venuto.
In past reported speech, 'as soon as he had finished' becomes non appena avesse finito, paired with sarebbe tornato.
Front a topic with di, then echo it with ne: Di soldi, ne ha fin troppi = as for money, he has far too much.
Che plus a subjunctive expresses a wish, English 'may...': Che Dio ti benedica = may God bless you.
Che plus a subjunctive can also issue an order, not just a wish: Che sia chiaro a tutti = let it be clear to everyone.
Sembra che signals uncertainty, so it takes the subjunctive: abbiano già preso, not 'hanno preso'.
Sembra che takes the subjunctive (abbia) even when the impression feels like plain fact.
Bisogna che needs the subjunctive: Bisogna che il cuoco prepari il menu = the cook needs to prepare the menu.
Prima che takes the subjunctive because the event hasn't happened yet: prima che i prezzi aumentino = before prices go up.
A 'the most... ever' phrase pulls in the subjunctive: il film più bello che io abbia mai visto.
Italian can't say 'want someone to do'; a wish about others needs che plus subjunctive: Voglio che si sentano amati.
When you front an object, the echoing pronoun is required, not sloppy: Questo libro, l'ho già letto.
Italian uses the future to guess about the past: Sarà stato mezzanotte = it must have been midnight.
A gerund at the front means 'since' or 'because': Essendo stanco = because he was tired.
Non è che softens a denial and takes the subjunctive: Non è che non voglia venire = it's not that I don't want to come.
Ne ha combinate di tutti i colori is literally 'pulled off ones of every color', meaning got up to every kind of mischief.
Avendo plus a participle packs the earlier event into one clause: Non avendo ricevuto risposta = not having received a reply.
Pur before a gerund flips it to 'although': Pur sapendo la verità = despite knowing the truth.
È auspicabile che, a formal 'it is hoped that', takes the subjunctive: che si trovino soluzioni condivise.
A bare past participle can open the sentence, no word for 'having' needed: Arrivato a casa = once he'd arrived home.
Vale la pena sottolineare is literally 'it's worth the pain to underline', a standard formula for adding emphasis.
Pair quanto più with tanto meno for 'the more... the less': Quanto più ci penso, tanto meno capisco.
The è... che frame spotlights one element: È proprio questo che volevo dire = THIS is what I wanted to say.
As a subject, Italian uses the plain infinitive where English uses -ing: Imparare una lingua = learning a language.
Sia che... sia che means 'whether... or', and both halves take the subjunctive: sia che piova sia che splenda.
Front a quantity with di, then resume it with ne: Di pazienza, ne servirà molta = of patience, a lot will be needed.
An infinitive can act as a noun, taking il, suo and adjectives: il suo continuo lamentarsi = his constant complaining.
An opening past participle agrees with its noun: Letta la lettera uses feminine letta to match la lettera.
Put il in front of an infinitive to make it a noun subject: Il vivere in città = living in the city.
In formal Italian a past participle can stand alone as a whole clause: Ciò premesso = that having been stated.
Fermo restando is literally 'remaining firm', a frozen legal opener meaning 'without prejudice to'.
L' before an infinitive turns it into a noun where English uses -ing: L'aver studiato = the having studied.
Per quanto means 'however much' and forces the subjunctive: per quanto la questione possa sembrare irrilevante.
Bisogna has no subject, so use Bisogna che plus subjunctive: Bisogna che io studi = I need to study.
Colloquial mica can replace non entirely: Mica male = not bad at all.
Senza che takes the subjunctive and pairs with nessuno where English says 'anyone': senza che nessuno se ne accorgesse.
Per la quale is the formal written version of per cui, and la quale agrees with feminine l'azienda.
Avendo plus a participle marks an action finished before the main verb: Avendo finito il lavoro = having finished work.
Purché means 'provided that' and always takes the subjunctive: Purché venga fatta giustizia = as long as justice is done.
Lungi is an archaic 'far' that survives only in this formula: Lungi dall'essere risolto = far from being resolved.
In Ce la metto tutta the ce and la are frozen bits of mettercela tutta; la points at nothing, and that's the trap.
Fare plus an infinitive means someone else does it for you: Ho fatto riparare la macchina = I had the car repaired.
Farcela means to manage or cope; here ce and la are fixed inside the verb and più adds 'anymore': Non ce la faccio più.
Prendersela means to get upset or take it personally; add con for the target: Se la prende con me.
A bare gerund covers English 'if' or 'by' with no separate word: Andando avanti così = if we go on like this.
